Roy Robinson [11:39 AM]
Hey Micha, were you notified regarding the trivy vuln?
[11:39 AM]
You and I are the only ones who had it: https://github.com/search?q=org%3Aslaclab%20aquasecurity%2Ftrivy-action&type=code
[11:40 AM]
CrowdStrike has identified a supply chain compromise involving the aquasecurity/trivy-action GitHub Action, a popular open-source vulnerability scanner used in CI/CD pipelines. This discovery was made while investigating an increase in script control detections across several Falcon customer environments. Our team found that attackers maliciously modified 76 out of 77 release tags by "repointing" them in git. These compromised tags now direct to a multi-stage credential theft payload. This payload executes before the legitimate scanner functionality runs, allowing the malicious activity to occur while the workflow appears to finish successfully. Adversaries also compromised Trivy version 0.69.4 by injecting malicious code that executes during the binary's runtime. AquaSecurity has officially confirmed the compromise of the Trivy GitHub Action script, setup script, and binary, and has subsequently removed all malicious artifacts from their repositories. Status: Active investigation in progress. This article will be updated as new information becomes available. Details CrowdStrike analyzed all 77 release tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action (versions 0.0.1 through 0.35.0) and identified the following: Am I impacted? If you use aquasecurity/trivy-action in your CI/CD pipelines, you are likely affected. You are impacted if: Your GitHub Actions workflows reference aquasecurity/trivy-action You are pinning to any version except 0.35.0 You are using tag-based references (e.g., @v0.34.0, @0.33.0) Presence of Trivy 0.69.4 binary in your environment. Github Actions workflows that reference the aquasecurity/setup-trivy action. (any version). What do customers need to do? Organizations using Trivy 0.69.4 should immediately verify binary integrity and update to a clean version. Check your workflows: Review your .github/workflows/ directory for any references to aquasecurity/trivy-action Identify which version/tag is specified If using any version other than 0.35.0, assume compromise Review your .github/workflows/ directory for any references to aquasecurity/setup-trivy (any version)
if i recall correctly, the shared mount will still require that a directory is created at the mountpoint that becomes the shared mount for the mounts. ie sharing /sdf/data/X will create a directory at /sdf/data/X/<pvc> and share that rather than the top level X directory which is what we want.
Performed an experimental merge of the upstream code with our modified branch. The merge conflicts in the critical `provisioner.go` code (attached) revealed that many changes had taken place, with some code that appeared to suggest that Shared Filesystem support had actually been officially added.
Indeed, some more code review shows that PR #183 added support for SharedFS, apparently explicitely geared towards allowing ReadWriteMany and ReadOnlyMany support for systems like ours where nodes are expected to mount shared filesystems on a consistent filepath:
https://github.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/pull/183
sharedFileSystemPath allows the provisioner to use a filesystem that is mounted on all nodes at the same time.
In this case all access modes are supported: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany and ReadWriteMany for storage claims.
In addition volumeBindingMode: Immediate can be used in StorageClass definition.
Please note that nodePathMap and sharedFileSystemPath are mutually exclusive. If sharedFileSystemPath is used, then nodePathMap must be set to [].
We will want to carefully inspect the current codebase to confirm that it will indeed meet our needs (which seems very likely at this point).
However, we MUST be careful planning, and testing, a migration back to the upstream codebase, in particular:
We need to update all PVs `reclaimPolicy` to be `Retain` (not `Delete)`, because we set this to Delete just to prevent proliferation of unused PVs (eg: here). Our custom branch had removed the code that actually deleted data, but the main branch would be expected to honor this.
The good news of course is that if indeed we can migrate back to the main upstream release branch, this will free us from maintaining our own fork, and allow us to more often and more easily update the image to incorporate fixes and new features.
